prompt: What do the three patterns of this lesson all do first?

choices.text: Create three folders: models, views and controllers
choices.why: Folders are a consequence some frameworks impose; a single file can follow the pattern.

choices.text: Move the rules into a model that knows nothing of screens
choices.why: Right. Fowler calls it separated presentation, and every pattern here starts with it.

choices.text: Make the view observe the model and redraw itself when it changes
choices.why: That is MVC's particular move; MVP's view never sees the model at all.

choices.text: Replace the keyboard with a web page
choices.why: The input device is one of the things that changes; the patterns let it change without touching the rules.

prompt: The library raises the loan limit from two to five. In tangled.py plus a web page written later, what is the likely result?

choices.text: Both update together, because they run on the same machine
choices.why: Running on one machine shares nothing; each has its own copy of the check.

choices.text: One copy of the check is changed and the other is missed
choices.why: Right. The web page could not reuse the loop, so it copied the rule, and two copies drift.

choices.text: The web page refuses to start until the terminal program is stopped
choices.why: Nothing ties the two processes together; that is exactly why the rule ends up written twice.

prompt: Match each change to the job of the program it touches.

pairs.left: A late return now costs 75 cents a day
The shelf list moves into a table with two columns
The desk is used from a phone instead of a keyboard

prompt: In mvc.py, the line lend B1 bia arrives. Put what happens in order.
items: The view prints the shelf line
The controller has the view say when B1 is due
trap: The controller does not draw the shelf: the view redraws inside the model's call, before lend returns.

prompt: Why does the model in desk_model.py raise ValueError instead of printing a message?

choices.text: Python forbids print inside a class method
choices.why: It does not; ShelfView.render prints from a method.

choices.text: An exception is faster than writing to the terminal
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it; the point is who decides what the person sees.

choices.text: It cannot know where its words will be shown, or if they will be
choices.why: Right. A terminal, a web page and a test each show a refusal differently, and the same model serves all three.

choices.text: So that the program stops when a loan is refused
choices.why: The controller catches it and the desk carries on with the next line, as the transcript shows.

prompt: A second view, a log that writes every change to a file, is added to mvc.py. What has to change in desk_model.py?

choices.text: Nothing at all: the log subscribes, like ShelfView
choices.why: Right. The desk calls whatever subscribed and does not know what it is.

choices.text: A call to the log inside lend and give_back
choices.why: That would make the model point at a view, which is the one arrow MVC never draws.

choices.text: A second list of watchers, one per kind of view
choices.why: One list holds any callable; the desk does not sort them by kind.

choices.text: An import of the log class, so the model can construct it
choices.why: The model never builds its observers; the main block does the wiring.

prompt: In web.py, which part plays the controller?

choices.text: shelf_page and message_page
choices.why: Those turn values into HTML; they are the views.

choices.text: show_shelf and lend, reached through ROUTES
choices.why: Right. Each reads the request, calls the model, and picks a view and a status.

choices.text: The Desk class, because it decides whether to lend
choices.why: Deciding the rules is the model's job, on the server as on the terminal.

prompt: Why does web.py never call desk.subscribe?

choices.text: WSGI applications are not allowed to hold Python objects between requests
choices.why: They can; the desk object itself survives between requests, which is how the shelf remembers the loan.

choices.text: A page already sent cannot be redrawn by the server
choices.why: Right. Each request renders from scratch; nothing is left to notify.

choices.text: The controllers are functions, and only classes may subscribe
choices.why: subscribe takes any callable; ShelfView passed a bound method.

choices.text: The desk only notifies when it runs inside a terminal
choices.why: The model knows nothing of terminals; it would call subscribers anywhere.

prompt: In the transcript of web.py, what HTTP status code did Caio's request for B1 receive?
In mvp.py, which class decides that a late return is shown as R$ 2,00?

choices.text: ConsoleView, because it is the class that prints
choices.why: ConsoleView prints the string it is given and formats nothing.

choices.text: Desk, because the fine is a rule of the library
choices.why: The amount is a rule; how 200 cents looks is presentation, and the model hands back a number.

choices.text: DeskPresenter
choices.why: Right. It calls money() and picks the alarm flag; the view only displays.

prompt: A new rule for the screen: a member's name is shown in capitals in every message. Where does the test for it go, in the MVP version?

choices.text: In a test that runs mvp.py and searches its printed output
choices.why: That is the MVC-style test the pattern exists to avoid; the decision lives where a fake view can see it.

choices.text: Beside the others in test_presenter.py, reading FakeView.messages
choices.why: Right. Capitalising is a decision about what the person sees, so it is the presenter's and its fake view records it.

choices.text: In a test of ConsoleView, since the view prints the name
choices.why: A passive view receives the finished text; if it capitalised, it would no longer be passive.

choices.text: In desk_model.py, since names belong to members
choices.why: Upper case is not a rule of the library; the model would then be deciding about screens.

prompt: In the form of MVP this lesson builds, Fowler's name for a view that only forwards events and shows what it is told is a ___ view.
What is the difference between a presenter and a view-model, in this lesson's programs?

choices.text: The presenter calls the view; the view-model does not know it exists
choices.why: Right. A view-model only exposes properties, and bindings carry them to the screen.

choices.text: Only the presenter can be tested without a screen
choices.why: The view-model is tested even more directly, with no fake view at all.

choices.text: The view-model reads the model and the presenter does not
choices.why: Both hold the model; DeskPresenter calls desk.lend just as LendViewModel does.

choices.text: It is the same object, renamed by Microsoft for WPF
choices.why: The arrows differ: one pushes into a view interface, the other is pulled by bindings.

prompt: In mvvm.py, typing B1 into the code box printed nothing at all. Why?

choices.text: The code box was not bound to the view-model yet when the typing happened
choices.why: It was bound before anybody typed; the value did reach vm.code.

choices.text: Nothing changed, so nothing was notified
choices.why: Right. With no member typed, the status stayed "type a code and a member", so Observable.set did nothing.

choices.text: The view-model ignores the code until a member is typed
choices.why: It recomputed at once; the result happened to be the same as before.

prompt: Which cost of MVVM does the section name first?

choices.text: Every widget needs a method in a view interface
choices.why: That is MVP's cost, the one bindings remove.

choices.text: The model has to import the view-model
choices.why: The model imports nothing of the screen; the view-model subscribes to it.

choices.text: The flow of updates is hard to follow
choices.why: Right. Why a button greyed out is answered by tracing subscriptions, not by reading one method.

choices.text: It needs a platform from Microsoft
choices.why: It began in WPF and lives in Android, Vue and Angular; mvvm.py runs on plain Python.

prompt: Match each pattern to who updates the screen.

pairs.right: the view, when the model notifies it
the controller, rendering a view per request
the presenter, by calling the view
the bindings, when a property changes

prompt: A class you have never seen exposes is_valid and error_text as properties, and nothing in it refers to any widget. Which pattern is it most likely part of?

choices.text: MVP, because it has no reference to the model
choices.why: A presenter would call the view, through methods like show_error; this class calls nobody.

choices.text: The original MVC, as its view
choices.why: A view draws; this class only holds state and knows no screen.

choices.text: MVVM, as a view-model
choices.why: Right. Properties for a screen to bind to, and no knowledge of the screen, is the shape of a view-model.

prompt: In the comparing section, how many times does grep -c find the word print in desk_model.py?
You are writing a desk application in Tkinter, which has no data binding worth the name, and the screen logic needs tests. What does the section suggest?

choices.text: MVVM, after writing a binding library first
choices.why: Possible, and then the binding library is a framework you maintain; the section points the other way.

choices.text: MVP, with a fake view in the tests
choices.why: Right. Two ordinary classes give testable screen logic where nothing binds.

choices.text: The web's MVC, with one route and one handler for each button on the form
choices.why: Routes answer HTTP requests; a desktop window has none.

prompt: When is tangled.py, with no separation at all, a reasonable design?

choices.text: Never: every program with output should separate presentation
choices.why: The section says the opposite for a script with one screen; separation before a second screen is speculation.

choices.text: When it is shorter than a hundred lines
choices.why: Size is not the test; a short script with two screens already pays the cost.

choices.text: While no second screen, test or redesign is actually coming
choices.why: Right. Those three are what the tangle costs, and until one is real it costs nothing.

choices.text: When the program runs only in a terminal
choices.why: mvc.py and mvp.py are terminal programs too, and earn their separation through tests.

prompt: Which of these are screen logic rather than rules of the library? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Showing 150 cents as R$ 1,50
choices.why: Right. The amount is the library's; the way it reads on screen is presentation.

choices.text: A member may hold at most five loans
choices.why: That is a rule, and it lives in Desk.lend whichever screen asks.

choices.text: Greying out the Lend button while the member is at the limit
choices.why: Right. The limit is a rule; what the button looks like because of it is screen logic, held by the view-model.

choices.text: A late return costs 50 cents a day
choices.why: A rule; give_back computes it and returns a number.

choices.text: Marking a refusal as an alarm
choices.why: Right. The presenter decides it; the refusal itself came from the model.

prompt: A Django project's views.py functions each open the database, check the loan limit and build the reply. What is wrong, in this lesson's terms?

choices.text: Django's views should be templates; the logic belongs in HTML
choices.why: Templates are the views of the table; putting the limit there would tangle it with the drawing instead.

choices.text: The controllers are doing the model's work, so the rule cannot be reused
choices.why: Right. Django's views are controllers; the limit belongs in a model a script or a test could call.

choices.text: Nothing: in Django the view is supposed to do everything
choices.why: Django calls them views, but the arrows are a controller's, and a controller should be three lines.

choices.text: It should be rewritten as MVVM, so that the screen binds straight to the database tables
choices.why: A server-rendered page has no live screen to bind; the fix is a thin controller over a model.

prompt: In all four programs of the lesson, the one file that never changed and never printed held the rules: it was the ___ .
